findings.claim: Essential Quotations Bank: Human response: “By ten o’clock the police organisation was lost in the growing pressure of the flight”
findings.truth: Fabricated. Wells writes: “By ten o’clock the police organisation, and by midday even the railway organisations, were losing coherency, losing shape and efficiency, guttering, softening, running at last in that swift liquefaction of the social body.” Replaced with the verbatim phrase “that swift liquefaction of the social body”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #36, Book One ch. 16 (The Exodus from London), lines 3213-3217 of scripts/_retrofc/_texts/war-of-the-worlds.txt

findings.claim: “The War of the Worlds question will appear on your 19th-century literature paper. It tests AO1..., AO2... and AO3 (context).” plus a Key Fact and revision tip naming “the three Assessment Objectives”.
findings.truth: Four Assessment Objectives are assessed on this question. AO4 (spelling and punctuation) is assessed in the 19th-century prose section, and is worth marks the unit never mentions anywhere. The paper is not a 19th-century literature paper either: its first section is the modern prose or drama question.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md section 3h: “Learners will be assessed on the use of a range of vocabulary and sentence structures... with accurate spelling and punctuation (AO4) in Section B of each examined component.” Section 3a: the paper is Exploring modern and literary heritage texts, 80 marks, 40 + 40.

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions across all 8 lessons carry type “40 marks — Shakespeare Essay”.
findings.truth: The War of the Worlds is a 19th-century prose set text. Shakespeare sits on the other paper. Relabelled “40 marks — 19th-century prose essay”. The 40-mark total is correct.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md sections 3a and the 19th century prose text list (The War of the Worlds — H G Wells).

findings.claim: 42 questions carry a six-band ladder with TWO bands both named “Top band” (35-40 and 29-34) and a non-house “Lower band (1-7)”; the 6 questions in lesson 1 carry only “Band 6 / Lower bands”. Eight of them read “Detailed analysis with AO2 and AO3.”
findings.truth: Rescaled every ladder to five equal house bands over 40 marks: Top band (33-40), Upper-mid band (25-32), Mid band (17-24), Lower-mid band (9-16), Low band (1-8). The question-specific top descriptor is kept. “AO2 and AO3.” also broke the house rule against an AO code immediately before a full stop.
findings.evidence: Unit mark total 40 (spec 3a); house band ladder per the checker brief.

findings.claim: “Before we judge them too harshly, we must remember what ruthless and utter destruction our own species has wrought.” Repeated in lesson 7 and four times in lesson 8, including the Key Quotations to Memorise list, a cloze flashcard and a matching item.
findings.truth: Wells writes “And before we judge of them too harshly we must remember what ruthless and utter destruction our own species has wrought”. The word “of” is dropped and a comma added. Corrected in all seven places.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #36, Book One ch. 1, lines 162-163 of the curated text.

findings.claim: A lesson titled “Book 1: The Fall of Civilisation”, described as Book 1 chapters 8-17, states that the Martians “also bring Red Weed, an alien plant that spreads rapidly across the landscape”.
findings.truth: The red weed does not appear in Book One. It is introduced in Book Two ch. 2 and spreads through Book Two. Reworded to place the spread in Book 2.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #36: BOOK TWO begins at line 4013; the first mention of the red weed is line 4515.

findings.claim: “Wells may be drawing on real anxieties about chemical warfare (the Hague Convention of 1899 attempted to ban poison gas)”, and a flashcard: “Fears of chemical warfare, addressed by the 1899 Hague Convention’s attempted ban on poison gas.”
findings.truth: The Hague Declaration on asphyxiating gases is 1899. The novel was serialised in 1897 and published as a book in 1898, so the convention cannot be a source. Reworded so the date order is explicit.
findings.evidence: Publication 1898 (stated in lesson 1); Hague Convention 1899.

findings.claim: <dfn> on “Social Darwinism” carries data-def “The pseudoscientific belief that selective breeding should be applied to humans to improve the species.”
findings.truth: That is the definition of eugenics. Social Darwinism applies ‘survival of the fittest’ to people and societies. The lesson body already says so, so the pop-up contradicted the paragraph it sits in.
findings.evidence: Lesson 4 n7 itself: “Social Darwinism — the idea that only the ‘fittest’ deserve to survive.”

findings.claim: <dfn> on “civilisation” carries data-def “The state of society when laws and social structures break down, leading to disorder.”
findings.truth: That defines the opposite of the word. Lesson 7 defines the same term correctly as “The established social structures, laws, institutions and norms that organise human society.” Corrected to match.
findings.evidence: Lesson 7 content_html, same term, correct definition.

findings.claim: “The British army responds with conventional weapons that prove completely ineffective.”
findings.truth: Not completely. Artillery destroys a Martian at Shepperton in Book One ch. 12, and the Thunder Child destroys two in ch. 17 — which lesson 3 of this same unit states. Softened to “almost always fail”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #36 Book One ch. 12 and ch. 17 (“‘Two!’ yelled the captain”, line 3969); lesson 3 n8.

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: “The 19th-century literature paper (Component 01).”
findings.truth: Carries a spec code (a banned string class) and misnames the paper, which also holds the modern prose or drama question. Replaced with “The modern and literary heritage paper — the 19th-century novel question.”
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/english-literature-J352.md section 3a.

findings.claim: Question stems built from the lesson topic slug: “How does Wells present character analysis in The War of the Worlds?” and “...in relation to character analysis.” Lesson 8 has the same fault with “exam technique”.
findings.truth: Neither is an answerable literary question; a student practising them would write about the wrong thing. Four stems rewritten to real topics (the narrator; the curate and the artilleryman; the fragility of civilisation; the novel as a whole).
findings.evidence: Practice question texts, lessons 5 and 8, items 0 and 1.

findings.claim: “the Heat-Ray devastates the Surrey militia” (twice).
findings.truth: No militia appears in the novel. The troops on Horsell Common are the Cardigan regiment and hussars, plus Maxim guns. Changed to “the soldiers on Horsell Common”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #36 lines 1191, 1249, 1802 (Cardigan regiment); “militia” occurs nowhere in the text.

findings.claim: <dfn> on “atheist” carries data-def “A belief system that rejects supernatural explanations in favour of science and reason.”
findings.truth: That describes rationalism or naturalism. An atheist is a person who does not believe any god exists. Corrected.
findings.evidence: Standard definition.

findings.claim: <dfn> on “British Empire” carries data-def “The policy of extending a country’s power through colonisation...”
findings.truth: That defines imperialism, which is already a separate glossary term in every lesson of this unit. Changed to define the Empire itself.
findings.evidence: glossary_terms in all 8 lessons already carry “imperialism”.

findings.claim: The Thunder Child “sacrifices itself to protect a steamship carrying refugees across the Channel”.
findings.truth: The action is off the Essex coast near the Blackwater, and the paddle steamer is bound for Ostend across the North Sea. Changed to “away from the Essex coast”.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #36 lines 3802, 3811, 3838 (Ostend), 3927 (Essex coast).

findings.claim: Flashcard answers “AO1.” and “AO2.”
findings.truth: A bare AO code immediately before a full stop is a banned pattern that makes the house validator reject the whole unit, so these two would block the rest of the edits landing. Expanded to “AO1 — personal response supported by textual references.” and “AO2 — analysis of the writer’s methods and their effects.”
findings.evidence: Checker brief, validator limits.

findings.claim: “HMS Thunder Child” in lesson 3 content, a knowledge check and a flashcard.
findings.truth: Wells never uses HMS. He writes “the torpedo ram, Thunder Child” and “the ironclad”. The HMS prefix comes from later adaptations. Not worth an edit; the ship, its type and its two kills are all correct.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #36 lines 3817, 3908.

findings.claim: Quotation bank: “slain by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth”.
findings.truth: Wells writes “slain, after all man’s devices had failed, by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth.” The lesson elides the middle clause with no ellipsis. Wording of the retained words is exact, so left alone.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #36 Book Two ch. 8, lines 5987-5988.

findings.claim: Lesson 7 is titled “Symbolism & Setting”, but its content_html is entirely themes (imperialism, evolution, religion, fragility of civilisation) and its description says “as key themes”. Lesson 8 is titled “Key Themes & Exam Technique”. Lesson 7’s own Key Takeaways (red weed, Surrey setting, darkness and emptiness) discuss symbolism that never appears in its body.
findings.truth: Either the title should become “Key Themes”, or the body should be rebuilt as symbolism and setting to match the takeaways. Titles are not editable through _edits.json, and the choice changes what the lesson teaches, so this is Tom’s call. Recommendation: retitle lesson 7 “Themes: Empire, Evolution and Collapse” and leave the body, then trim lesson 8 to exam technique.
findings.evidence: Lesson 7 content_html vs conclusion_html; lesson 8 title.

findings.claim: “The Brother’s Perspective (Book 1, Chapters 14–17)” in lesson 5, and the same range in lesson 6.
findings.truth: The brother narrates ch. 14, 16 and 17. Ch. 15 (What Had Happened in Surrey) returns to the main narrator. The range is a shade wide but not misleading, so left alone.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #36 contents list, lines 47-67.

findings.claim: “Wells, an atheist” in lessons 5 and 7, and a flashcard “He was an atheist”.
findings.truth: Defensible but flattened. Wells left Christianity early, argued for a finite personal God in God the Invisible King (1917), then returned to atheism. For an 1898 novel the shorthand holds, so no edit; worth knowing if a student is challenged on it.
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._G._Wells

findings.claim: Lesson 4 says the narrator “is forced to knock him unconscious” and never says the curate dies.
findings.truth: Book Two ch. 4 is titled The Death of the Curate: the blow leads to his death and a handling-machine drags the body out. A lesson 1 flashcard does say “eventually killed”, so the unit is not wrong, only incomplete. Adding the death would change narration block n2; flagged rather than edited.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #36 contents, Book Two ch. IV.

summary: No lesson is clean: every one of the 48 practice questions was labelled a Shakespeare essay and carried a malformed six-band ladder with two bands called Top band. On top of that, lesson 8 carries a fabricated quotation in its memorisation bank and teaches only three Assessment Objectives when AO4 is assessed on this question, and the imperialism quotation is misworded in three lessons. 123 edits written; four items left for Tom, of which the lesson 7 title mismatch is the one that needs a decision.
